claims.text: A pull request names a source branch and a target branch and proposes the merge; opening one does not perform the merge.
claims.source_hint: GitHub Docs, Pull requests — About pull requests

claims.text: Git supplies the branch and the merge; the page carrying the diff, the review comments and the approval is supplied by the service hosting the repository, not by Git itself.
claims.source_hint: git-scm.com/docs full command list (no review or approval command); GitHub Docs, About pull request reviews

claims.text: Code review serves three ends at once: finding defects, moving knowledge in both directions between author and reviewer, and keeping the codebase consistent. Treating defects as the only purpose is what makes a review feel like an exam.
claims.source_hint: outline item 1 of the lesson entry in content/tracks/management/track.yaml

claims.text: On a team that grades comments this way, a must-fix holds the merge until the team settles it; a suggestion, a question and praise do not hold it, though the author answers every one. The grades are plain text: a hosting service can require an approval before a merge but cannot tell them apart.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/review-comments-examples.md lines 7, 11, 14, 18, 26, 31 — the file grades good comments, faults an ungraded one, and tells the author to answer each

claims.text: A question asks before it asserts because the reviewer may have misread; by itself it says nothing is wrong, though the author still owes it an answer.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/review-comments-examples.md lines 7-9 and 14-16, both of which ask rather than assert

claims.text: Approval means the change may merge, not that it cannot be improved; when a reviewer holds a change for preferences they could have marked as suggestions, the branch waits and collects conflicts.
